1.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how to translate the names in this book.

4.note: The ancient Greek translation reads, “The sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” You may wish to use that in your translation as an alternative reading, especially if a translation of the Bible exists in your region and it uses that reading.

6.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “Diphath.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “Riphath.” That is consistent with Genesis 10:3 If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

10.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he began** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the identify of **Nimrod** as the first man to become a **warrior**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he was the one who first became a warrior]

19.note: The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Eber had two sons]

19.q: שֵׁ֣ם הָ⁠אֶחָ֞ד פֶּ֗לֶג כִּ֤י בְ⁠יָמָי⁠ו֙ נִפְלְגָ֣ה הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ
19.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since the earth was divided in the days of the one, he named him Peleg]
The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during his lifetime]

Here, **the earth** represents the people of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth were divided]

The expression **was divided** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. This is a reference to the way Yahweh divided the people of the earth into separate groups by making them speak different languages, as Genesis 11:1–91 describes. Alternate translation: [Yahweh divided the people of the earth into separate groups]

Since the author mentions **Peleg** first, it seems likely that **Joktan** was his younger brother. If your language specifies whether a brother or sister is younger or older, you can do that in your translation, here and wherever the context makes it clear. Alternate translation: [his younger brother]

29.note: In this context, the abstract noun **generations** does not refer to all the people who were living at certain times. It describes the children, grandchildren, and further descendants that Isaac and Ishamel had. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [their descendants]

41.note: The author is using the plural term **sons** even though he only names one son of Anah. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a singular term here and in similar instances in the book. Alternate translation: [The son of Anah: Dishon]

43.note: The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before a king reigned]
The author is using the term **sons** to mean the “descendants” of **Israel**. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

45.note: The author is not referring to a specific **Temanite**. He means the Temanites, the inhabitants of the region of Teman, in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Temanites]

46.note: The author is using the name of the nation of **Midian** to refer to the army of that nation. Alternate translation: [the one having struck the Midianite army]

The author is speaking as if **Hadad** had hit this opposing army, but he means that he defeated it. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the introduction to 1 Chronicles. Alternate translation: [the one who defeated the Midianite army]
The author is using the term **field** to describe the land or territory of Moab, since there was much fertile agricultural area in that land. Alternate translation: [in the land of Moab]
